section_summary: This section is dominated by public and congressional protests over continued U.S. exports of petroleum, gasoline, scrap metal, aluminum, and other strategic materials to Japan, together with State Department acknowledgments and explanations of the export-licensing system. It also contains diplomatic and intelligence reporting on Japanese efforts to obtain manganese, rubber, scrap iron, cobalt, vanadium, cotton, and ores from India, Southeast Asia, Mexico, and Bolivia. The correspondence traces the expansion of petroleum controls through June 1941 and includes later replies referring to the July freezing of Japanese assets.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Lancaster on trade with Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides published trade statistics in response to an inquiry about Japanese purchases of American war materials.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Mrs. Lancaster's May 24 letter, referred by the Navy Department. It encloses a Department of Commerce publication covering U.S. exports to and imports from Japan through March 1941.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of R. H. Claypool's letter
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent's protest about strategic exports for consideration and report.
subfiles.summary: The Senate office forwards an enclosure and requests favorable consideration. The enclosure is R. H. Claypool's letter concerning oil, scrap iron, and other supplies reaching potential enemies.

subfiles.title: R. H. Claypool to Senator Tom Connally
subfiles.about: Protests American exports of oil, scrap iron, and other war supplies to Axis countries.
subfiles.summary: Claypool argues that national-defense spending and compulsory military service are inconsistent with private exports that strengthen potential enemies. Recalling his First World War service and recent observations at Texas ports, he calls for Congress to make capital and labor share the sacrifices imposed on soldiers.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Connally concerning Claypool
subfiles.about: Explains petroleum export controls and disputes claims of unrestricted gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that high-octane aviation fuel and lubricants had been restricted since July 26, 1940, and that licensing had expanded to nearly all gasoline. License applications were evaluated for their effects on national defense and controls were continually adjusted. It states that official Commerce Department statistics contradict the newspaper allegations cited by Claypool and returns his letter and editorial.

subfiles.title: Senator Hayden forwards H. F. McGinley's complaint
subfiles.about: Requests a full explanation of reported diesel-oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hayden encloses a letter from H. F. McGinley and a related clipping. He asks the Secretary of State to advise him fully about the reported shipments.

subfiles.title: H. F. McGinley to Senator Hayden
subfiles.about: Questions why the United States supports China while permitting large fuel-oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: McGinley cites a Los Angeles Times clipping and information from a West Coast shipping employee about Japanese vessels loading oil labeled as motor products. He argues that financing China while supplying Japan with fuel is incomprehensible to taxpayers.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Senator Hayden
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Hayden's inquiry concerning H. F. McGinley's complaint.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Hayden's May 29 letter and McGinley's enclosure. He promises prompt attention to the reported oil shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Substantive reply to Senator Hayden on oil exports
subfiles.about: Describes petroleum licensing rules applicable to shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull reviews the July 1940 restrictions on high-octane aviation fuel and lubricants and the later extension of licensing to other petroleum products. He states that applications are denied when shipments would harm national defense and that controls are continually revised. McGinley's letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Unidentified Oakland letter on supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Raises concerns about continued American supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded text appears to object to the continuing supply of materials to Japan. The writer asks for advice or an explanation, but much of the wording and the sender's identity are illegible.

subfiles.title: YWCA of Chicago urges an embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Lilace Reid Barnes, Young Women's Christian Association of Chicago
subfiles.about: Urges prohibition of all exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Barnes reports that a substantial majority in a 285-member poll supported a complete embargo because Japan was the aggressor in the Far East. The Metropolitan Board of Directors unanimously concluded that existing export controls were inadequate and asked the Department to prohibit all war-material exports.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lilace Reid Barnes on strategic exports
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains the export-control system in response to the Chicago YWCA's embargo appeal.
subfiles.summary: Allen states that proclaimed defense materials were subject to licensing under the Export Control Act of July 2, 1940. Exports to the British Empire and Western Hemisphere were generally allowed from available surpluses, while aviation gasoline and scrap iron were barred from other destinations and other licenses were issued sparingly. He encloses the July 1940 proclamation, regulations, and press release.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting manganese shipment to Japan
subfiles.to: Department of State and National Defense Commission
subfiles.about: Reports a large manganese shipment from Mormugao to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram states that three thousand tons of manganese were shipped from Mormugao on May 30 for Japan. A copy was routed to the defense authorities.

subfiles.title: Forwarding letter enclosing Richard Gurley's protest
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter from Richard Gurley for the secretary's consideration.
subfiles.summary: The writer encloses a copy of a letter received from Richard Gurley of St. Martin's Church in Radnor, Pennsylvania. The enclosure concerns American assistance to countries regarded as potential enemies.

subfiles.title: Richard Gurley letter opposing aid to potential enemies
subfiles.about: Condemns supplying materials that enable hostile powers to conduct war more effectively.
subfiles.summary: Gurley calls the practice of helping hostile powers improve their war-making capacity damnable and treacherous. He criticizes the absence of organized protest and the failure of the War, Navy, and State Departments to stop or condemn it.

subfiles.title: Amy H. Dowe appeals for an end to oil exports
subfiles.about: Asks the Department to stop Socony-Vacuum and other companies from exporting oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dowe says that she protested to Socony-Vacuum's president as a shareholder but was told that only the government could halt the trade. She rejects the argument that an oil embargo would endanger American access to East Indian rubber and urges reliance on synthetic substitutes.

subfiles.title: Representative Beckworth requests petroleum-export information
subfiles.about: Requests information on companies supplying oil to Japan and oil reaching the Axis from South America.
subfiles.summary: Beckworth asks which companies had supplied Japan with oil during the preceding months. He also requests the most comprehensive available report on petroleum moving from South America to the Axis powers.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Representative Beckworth
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Beckworth's inquiry about petroleum exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Beckworth's June 4 letter. He states that the request will receive prompt attention.

subfiles.title: Reply directing Beckworth to the Commerce Department
subfiles.about: Directs an inquiry about oil exports to the agency compiling American trade statistics.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that information about the origin and amounts of U.S. petroleum exports and other American republics' trade with Japan is collected by the Department of Commerce. He suggests that Beckworth address his statistical inquiry to that department.

subfiles.title: Ernest D. Vanderburgh questions aviation-gasoline exports
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japan still receives gasoline suitable for military aviation.
subfiles.summary: Vanderburgh reports hearing that only the highest grade of aviation fuel had been withheld and that Japan could still obtain gasoline comparable to that used by Germany. Although generally supportive of administration foreign policy, he calls continued petroleum exports an obvious inconsistency.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ernest D. Vanderburgh
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains licensing restrictions on petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allen reviews restrictions on high-octane aviation fuel and lubricants and the extension of licensing to other petroleum products. He says applications are assessed from multiple perspectives, denied when harmful to national defense, and governed by controls that change with conditions.

subfiles.title: Senator Brown forwards Jack J. Lande's second letter
subfiles.about: Requests comment on a renewed constituent complaint about oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Brown notes that he previously forwarded a May 22 inquiry from Jack J. Lande and sent the Department's answer to him. He now encloses Lande's follow-up letter and asks that it be returned with the Department's comments.

subfiles.title: Jack J. Lande's follow-up on oil shipments
subfiles.about: Complains that the State Department described licensing without explaining why petroleum was still shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lande says the earlier reply did not answer his central question about continuing oil exports. Citing a statement attributed to Maliki of the Honolulu Oil Company, he warns against appeasing Japan with oil and compares the policy to Munich.

subfiles.title: Reply returning Lande's letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges and returns Jack J. Lande's follow-up complaint.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Brown's June 4 letter. He states that Lande's comments have been carefully noted and returns the enclosure as requested.

subfiles.title: G. E. Tilton requests an explanation of Japan policy
subfiles.about: Asks how continued strategic exports to Japan can be reconciled with American support for China.
subfiles.summary: Tilton describes years of oil, scrap iron, machinery, and other materials leaving Pacific ports for Japan despite its war in China. He argues that limited embargoes appear ineffective and that Japan could attack American interests and citizens. He requests an explanation that would help him answer growing public criticism of the administration.

subfiles.title: Reply to G. E. Tilton on strategic-material controls
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, Department of State
subfiles.about: Describes export licensing and encloses regulations governing strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: Allen states that defense articles were subject to licensing and that exports outside the British Empire and Western Hemisphere were issued sparingly. He assures Tilton that controls were adjusted daily and no exports were allowed when national interests would be jeopardized. Copies of the July 1940 proclamation, regulations, and related announcements are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Tom Huston to President Roosevelt on the oil enigma
subfiles.about: Protests the apparent contradiction between aiding China and allowing oil and gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Huston first criticizes the administration's handling of defense-industry strikes, then encloses a Miami Herald editorial titled The Oil Enigma. He says the allegations caused him and his wife to reconsider purchasing Defense Bonds. He asks for a simple confirmation or denial that American oil and gasoline are helping Japanese attacks on China.

subfiles.title: Tom Huston's supplemental letter to Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Asks whether American-trained pilots might face Japanese weapons made or fueled with American materials.
subfiles.summary: Huston reacts to reports that American Army and Navy personnel might train Chinese flyers. He asks whether Americans could confront Japanese aircraft made with American steel and gasoline and condemns democratic governments for hesitation and weakness.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Tom Huston
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, Department of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Huston's letters by explaining petroleum export controls.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Huston's June 3 and June 5 letters, referred by the White House. Allen outlines restrictions on aviation fuel and lubricants and the extension of licensing to other petroleum products. He says applications are rejected when detrimental to national defense and controls are continually adjusted.

subfiles.title: Representative O'Brien forwards Ankenbrandt's letter
subfiles.about: Requests the Department's position on a constituent's complaint about gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: O'Brien encloses a letter from Stephen W. Ankenbrandt, whom he describes as a well-educated and substantial constituent. He asks for the State Department's attitude toward the question raised.

subfiles.title: Stephen W. Ankenbrandt to Representative O'Brien
subfiles.about: Endorses a Detroit News clipping concerning gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ankenbrandt encloses a Detroit News clipping and says it reflects his views. He believes many other people share the same sentiment.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Representative O'Brien
subfiles.about: Acknowledges O'Brien's letter and the Ankenbrandt enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of O'Brien's June 10 communication. He promises prompt attention to the concern about gasoline shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Detailed reply to Representative O'Brien
subfiles.about: Explains petroleum licensing and distinguishes East Coast gasoline shortages from Pacific export shipments.
subfiles.summary: Hull says most petroleum products, including high-octane fuel, were prohibited from export without a license and that the rule applied to Japan. Applications were rejected when detrimental to national defense and controls were continually revised. He adds that prospective Eastern gasoline curtailment was chiefly a transportation problem unrelated to Pacific Coast exports in foreign vessels and returns Ankenbrandt's letter.

subfiles.title: Representative Engel forwards Rex L. Ames's letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's question about gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Engel transmits an enclosed letter from Rex L. Ames of Muskegon. The surviving text is faint, but the enclosure concerns reports of gasoline shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Rex L. Ames protests gasoline shipments
subfiles.about: Questions reports that large quantities of gasoline were being shipped from San Pedro to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ames says he would willingly stop driving to conserve gasoline for the United States but not to benefit Japan. He asks Engel to explain the apparent contradiction and notes that he also wrote to the secretary of the interior.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Representative Engel
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Engel's referral of Rex L. Ames's gasoline complaint.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Engel's June 10 letter and the Ames enclosure. He promises prompt attention to the reported gasoline shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Representative Engel on petroleum controls
subfiles.about: Explains the June 20 extension of licensing to all petroleum products and discusses regional gasoline supply.
subfiles.summary: Welles states that most petroleum exports had long required licenses and that all petroleum products came under licensing on June 20, 1941. He says cases were evaluated for national-defense effects and policy was continually revised. Eastern shortages were primarily a transportation issue, while consumers' interests would be considered when licensing Atlantic Coast exports; Ames's letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on Southeast Asian rubber allocations
subfiles.about: Relays British proposals to reduce rubber supplies available to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Thailand allotted Japan 30,000 tons of rubber and offered the remaining 18,000 tons to Malaya if tin exports remained uncontrolled. The British minister suggested that Malaya stop supplying Japan and that Netherlands Indies shipments be reduced to a minimum. London was urged to consult the Netherlands government and the British consul general at Batavia to alert Van Mook.

subfiles.title: Square Deal Bosch inquiry about oil exports
subfiles.from: Manuel J. Bosch, Square Deal Bosch, Inc.
subfiles.to: State Department, Department of Export Licenses
subfiles.about: Asks whether oil and high-octane gasoline were being exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bosch says a discussion group had divided sharply over the question of oil exports. He asks the Department to state the exact status of shipments of petroleum and high-octane gasoline to Japan and other countries.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department statistics on petroleum exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports monthly quantities of U.S. petroleum exports to Japan from October 1940 through March 1941.
subfiles.summary: The letter lists monthly shipments ranging from about 1.34 million to 2.91 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products. It states that the shipments appeared to fall outside controls then limited chiefly to high-octane aviation gasoline. A summary of Roosevelt's May 2 press conference says gasoline sent to Japan was classified as lower-octane, non-aviation fuel.

subfiles.title: Clearance of report opposing H.R. 4824
subfiles.from: Acting Director, name and agency unclear
subfiles.about: Approves submission of an unfavorable report on legislation barring petroleum cargoes to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The acting director returns a proposed report to the House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries concerning H.R. 4824. The proposed report opposed enactment of the bill, which would prohibit vessel clearance for petroleum cargoes bound for Japan or its possessions, and the sender raises no objection to its submission.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the embassy in Santiago on Japanese plans
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the under secretary
subfiles.about: Directs the ambassador to approach Chile about reported Japanese plans.
subfiles.summary: The cable refers to the ambassador's second letter of May 12 and instructs him to approach the Chilean government along the previously indicated lines. He is asked to report the results, and the message is marked for careful paraphrase before disclosure.

subfiles.title: Harry T. Howard asks Roosevelt about butane gasoline
subfiles.about: Asks why the United States permits the sale of butane gasoline to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Howard, pastor of Jefferson Avenue Methodist Church in Detroit, sends a brief inquiry to the president. He asks for an explanation of the government's permission for gasoline sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Harry T. Howard
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains petroleum controls and the effect of freezing Japanese assets.
subfiles.summary: The Department outlines the licensing system for aviation fuel, lubricants, and other petroleum products and says applications are denied when contrary to national defense. It encloses a July 25 press release on the freezing of Japanese assets. The reply explains that the freeze effectively placed all export transactions involving Japanese interests under government control.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Bolivian exports to Japan
subfiles.to: Alan Goodrich Kirk and Sherman Miles
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese purchases and shipments of Bolivian minerals, cotton, and other commodities.
subfiles.summary: Hoover reports that Mauricio Hochschild, prominent in Bolivian minerals and recent tin negotiations, was among the leading sellers to Japan. The letter lists 1941 shipments of cotton, ores, and other commodities and says Japanese buyers were seeking further purchases and transshipment opportunities. Copies went to naval and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Bangkok telegram on Japanese scrap-iron purchases
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese purchases of scrap iron in Thailand and prospective Thai trade with Germany via Siberia.
subfiles.summary: Grant relays a Reuters report that Japanese agents had recently bought 100,000 tons of scrap iron and were searching Thailand for all available scrap. The press also reported Soviet permission for Thai use of the Trans-Siberian Railway and preparations by Thai merchants to export goods to Germany over that route.

subfiles.title: Coast Guard report on Japanese-Mexican communications
subfiles.to: Treasury, State, military, naval, customs, and FBI recipients
subfiles.about: Reproduces an intercepted commercial message concerning Japanese purchases of strategic materials in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The intercepted message directs rapid contracting and shipment of cobalt and vanadium through associates including Yamaguchi, Kobayashi, Fujii, and Nii, with prices quoted free on board Manzanillo. It also discusses remittances, branch credentials, Japanese commercial publications, and an awaited offer for gasoline and lubricating oil. The source is rated reliable and the report is distributed to several intelligence and enforcement agencies.

subfiles.title: Representative Boggs requests an explanation of oil policy
subfiles.about: Requests information to answer constituents protesting continued oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Boggs reports receiving many communications questioning why the government still allows petroleum exports to Japan. He encloses a clipping about a Standard Oil Company of New Jersey agreement for additional sales and notes criticism of the policy on the House floor. He asks for any nonconfidential explanation that he can provide to constituents.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Representative Boggs
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Boggs's inquiry about oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Boggs's June 11 letter. He promises prompt attention to the requested explanation of petroleum-export policy.

subfiles.title: Final reply to Boggs on statutory export controls
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory authority and administration of petroleum export licensing.
subfiles.summary: Welles reviews section 6 of the July 2, 1940 national-defense act and the president's authority to prohibit or curtail exports of military-related goods. He identifies Brigadier General Russell L. Maxwell as administrator of export control and explains the secretary of state's licensing role. The reply notes that most petroleum exports had required licenses since July 26, 1940, all petroleum products were covered from June 20, 1941, and licenses were denied when inconsistent with U.S. foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Alternate draft reply to Hale Boggs
subfiles.about: Provides an alternate formulation of the Department's explanation of petroleum export controls.
subfiles.summary: The draft again reviews the president's statutory authority, Russell L. Maxwell's administrative role, and the secretary of state's case-by-case licensing decisions. It states that all petroleum products became subject to licensing on June 20 and assures Boggs that exports inconsistent with U.S. foreign policy would not be licensed.

subfiles.title: Senator Brown forwards Dale O. Miller's questions
subfiles.about: Requests answers to a Detroit businessman's questions about exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Brown encloses a letter from Dale O. Miller, president of Simplex Engineering Corporation. He asks for the Department's comments before acknowledging Miller and requests return of the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Dale O. Miller challenges gasoline and aluminum exports
subfiles.about: Poses a series of hostile questions about gasoline and aluminum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miller asks whether high-test gasoline sent to Japan was re-exported to Germany, used against China, and licensed by the State Department. He contrasts alleged exports with Sunday driving restrictions and aluminum shortages affecting his government-contract foundry. The letter broadens into criticism of defense-industry strikes, John L. Lewis, William Green, and federal labor policy.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Brown on Miller's export questions
subfiles.about: Explains controls over petroleum and aluminum exports in response to Dale O. Miller.
subfiles.summary: Welles reviews the president's export-control authority and Russell L. Maxwell's role in administering it. He states that most petroleum products and nearly all forms and derivatives of aluminum required licenses, with all petroleum products covered from June 20. Miller's letter is returned after an assurance that the issues he raised were carefully considered before licenses were issued.

subfiles.title: Later reply concerning Dale O. Miller
subfiles.about: Answers a later Miller letter about British aircraft, aluminum toys, and petroleum controls.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the Department has no information that Britain recently delivered aircraft to South America for commercial or private use or shipped aluminum toys to Chicago department stores. He notes the president's August 2 announcement of new petroleum-export regulations and encloses the relevant press release. Miller's July 14 letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Brown's original Miller referral
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Dale O. Miller's letter about oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Brown's June 11 referral. He promises prompt attention to Miller's complaint concerning oil shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Senator Mead's referral of R. H. Hood's letter
subfiles.from: Office of Senator James M. Mead
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent inquiry about oil and gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mead's office forwards an enclosure for favorable consideration. It requests a report to accompany the return of R. H. Hood's letter.

subfiles.title: R. H. Hood asks about gasoline shipments
subfiles.about: Asks whether oil or gasoline was still being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hood asks Mead for a direct answer about continued petroleum shipments. He sarcastically contrasts possible Sunday driving restrictions in the United States with Japan's use of fuel for bombing China.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Senator Mead
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Mead's referral of R. H. Hood's inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Mead's June 14 communication and Hood's letter. He promises prompt attention to the question of oil and gasoline shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Final reply to Senator Mead on petroleum exports
subfiles.about: Explains petroleum licensing and the distinction between export shipments and prospective Eastern gasoline curtailment.
subfiles.summary: Welles directs Mead to the Department of Commerce for statistical data on exports to Japan. He explains that most petroleum products already required licenses and that all petroleum products came under control on June 20. The reply says applications were denied when detrimental to national defense, distinguishes Eastern transportation shortages from Pacific Coast exports, and promises that domestic consumers' interests would be considered in licensing Atlantic Coast shipments.
